title: Half of NASA’s Aging Mars Fleet Goes Dark Amid Technical Glitches, Ars Technica Reports
body:
NASA’s two longest‑serving Mars orbiters are now facing critical setbacks that could curtail their scientific output for the remainder of their missions. The Perseverance rover, which has been sending high‑resolution images and atmospheric data back to Earth since its landing in February 2021, is experiencing a serious communications glitch that has forced engineers to suspend most of its data‑downlink activities. At the same time, the orbiting spacecraft Odyssey, launched in 2001 and still operating after more than two decades, is rapidly depleting its dwindling supply of hydrazine fuel, raising concerns that its ability to maintain the precise orbital adjustments needed for its mapping duties may soon be compromised.

The communications issue with Perseverance appears to stem from a malfunction in the rover’s high‑gain antenna system, which is responsible for transmitting large volumes of data directly to NASA’s Deep Space Network. While the rover’s low‑gain antenna remains functional enough to receive commands, the reduced bandwidth severely limits the amount of scientific data that can be relayed. Mission controllers have switched to a “store‑and‑forward” mode, buffering data for later transmission when the antenna can be re‑enabled, but the backlog is already growing. Scientists fear that time‑sensitive observations—such as seasonal changes in the Martian climate and ongoing experiments with the rover’s MOXIE oxygen‑production unit—could be delayed or missed altogether.

Odyssey’s predicament is equally worrisome, albeit for a different reason. The spacecraft relies on a finite reserve of hydrazine propellant to perform regular trajectory correction maneuvers that keep it in a stable, low‑altitude orbit ideal for high‑resolution mapping of the planet’s surface and subsurface. Recent telemetry indicates that the remaining fuel is being consumed at a faster rate than anticipated, a situation attributed to a combination of aging thruster performance and the need for more frequent adjustments to counteract atmospheric drag. With the fuel budget projected to be exhausted within the next few Earth months, NASA engineers are evaluating a “fuel‑saving” profile that would reduce the frequency of orbit‑maintenance burns, albeit at the cost of lower-resolution data and reduced coverage of certain scientific targets.

Both setbacks highlight the challenges inherent in operating spacecraft far beyond their designed lifespans. Perseverance, built on a robust chassis and equipped with cutting‑edge instrumentation, was never intended to serve as a long‑term communications relay for future missions. Its current issue underscores the importance of redundancy in deep‑space hardware, especially as NASA plans to expand its presence on the Red Planet with upcoming sample‑return missions and the Artemis‑led lunar gateway. Meanwhile, Odyssey’s dwindling fuel stock serves as a stark reminder that even the most durable orbiters require careful resource management; the spacecraft’s continued success has hinged on meticulous planning and periodic software updates that have stretched its operational envelope far beyond the original 12‑year mission plan.

NASA’s response to the twin crises involves a blend of immediate troubleshooting and strategic reprioritization. For Perseverance, engineers are conducting a series of diagnostic commands to isolate the faulty antenna component, exploring the possibility of reconfiguring the rover’s existing hardware to bypass the defect. In parallel, the agency is leveraging other assets—such as the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and the newly arrived Mars Sample Return lander—to fill the data gap, ensuring that critical observations are not entirely lost. Regarding Odyssey, mission planners are considering a “low‑fuel” operational mode that would focus on high‑value scientific objectives while accepting a reduced mapping cadence. This approach could extend the spacecraft’s functional life by several months, buying time for the next generation of orbital platforms to assume its role.

Looking ahead, NASA’s experience with aging Mars assets is shaping the architecture of future interplanetary missions. The agency is now emphasizing modular designs that allow for in‑situ repairs or upgrades, as well as more robust fault‑tolerant communication systems that can sustain long‑duration operations. The lessons learned from Perseverance’s antenna failure and Odyssey’s fuel depletion will inform the development of the Mars Sample Return campaign slated for the late 2020s, ensuring that critical data streams remain uninterrupted. While the current challenges impose short‑term constraints, they also provide valuable insight into how humanity can maintain a resilient presence on Mars, even as hardware ages and resources dwindle.
